t: Hebrew, a Canaanite language of the Iron Age kingdoms of Israel and Judah, is the language of most of the Hebrew Bible, written and edited over many centuries in the 1st millennium BCE.

Displaced in daily life by Aramaic, Greek and later other languages, it lived on for nearly two thousand years as the language of Jewish prayer, law, poetry, philosophy and correspondence across the world.
Revived as a spoken language from the late 19th century, it is today the language of Israel and of some 9 million speakers, a unique case of a language reborn as the mother tongue of a nation.
dyk: Ben-Zion Ben-Yehuda, born in Jerusalem in 1882 and raised by his father Eliezer to speak only Hebrew, is often called the first native speaker of the language in modern times.
ev: The Gezer calendar, one of the oldest inscriptions in a Hebrew or related Canaanite dialect, lists the months of the farming year
The Siloam inscription records the cutting of a water tunnel under Jerusalem
The Mishnah, the code of Jewish law, is compiled in Mishnaic Hebrew
The Aleppo Codex, a masterpiece of the Masoretic text with its vowel signs, is written in Tiberias
Eliezer Ben-Yehuda settles in Jerusalem and begins his campaign to revive spoken Hebrew
The British Mandate for Palestine recognises Hebrew as an official language beside English and Arabic
The first Dead Sea Scrolls, including the oldest known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible, are found near Qumran
Israel founds the Academy of the Hebrew Language

f.family: Afroasiatic: the Canaanite group of the Northwest Semitic languages, close to Phoenician and Moabite
f.script: The Paleo-Hebrew alphabet, derived from the Phoenician; after the Babylonian exile, the Aramaic “square script” still used today
f.earliest: Inscriptions of the 10th and 9th centuries BCE, such as the Gezer calendar, whose language is debated; the Siloam inscription of about 700 BCE
f.status: Revived as a spoken language from the late 19th century; the official language of Israel, spoken by some 9 million people
